title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
summary: JSON is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format derived from ECMAScript. It defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data. This document removes inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON and was replaced by RFC 8259.

plainLanguage.summary: JSON is a way of writing data as text so that programs in any language can read it. It has six kinds of value: an object, an array, a string, a number, and the two booleans, plus null. This revision tidies up the earlier specification so that two programs reading the same text agree on what it means, and warns about the places where implementations used to differ.

subtitle: A small, text-based way to write structured data that any programming language can read.

tldr.problem: Applications written in different languages needed a common way to exchange structured data, and the earlier description of JSON left a few gaps that caused real interoperability problems between implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a complete grammar for JSON, a value being an object, an array, a string, a number, or one of three literal names, plus rules on encoding, on the treatment of unpaired surrogates and on what parsers and generators must do.
tldr.outcome: The document removes the inconsistencies, applies two errata, and adds experience-based guidance on the practices that lead to interoperability failures. RFC 7159 was obsoleted by RFC 8259.

today: RFC 7159 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 8259.

sections.title: What JSON Is
sections.content:
JSON is a text format for the serialization of structured data. It is derived from the object literals of JavaScript, as defined in the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard, Third Edition. The terms object and array come from the conventions of JavaScript.

JSON can represent four primitive types, strings, numbers, booleans and null, and two structured types, objects and arrays. A string is a sequence of zero or more Unicode characters. An object is an unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs, where a name is a string and a value is a string, number, boolean, null, object or array. An array is an ordered sequence of zero or more values.

The design goals for JSON were that it be minimal, portable, textual, and a subset of JavaScript. This document updates RFC 4627, which described JSON and registered the media type application/json. A description of JSON in ECMAScript terms also appears in Version 5.1 of the ECMAScript specification, and JSON is separately described in ECMA-404, and all of the specifications of JSON syntax agree on the syntactic elements of the language.

The reason for this revision is that in the years since RFC 4627 was published, JSON found very wide use, and that experience revealed certain patterns which, while allowed by the specifications, caused interoperability problems. A small number of errata had also been reported. The goal of this document is to apply the errata, remove inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON, and highlight practices that can lead to interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: JSON grew out of JavaScript's way of writing object literals, and it was designed to stay small enough to read easily, to be pure text, and to travel between any two programs. This version exists because wide use exposed a handful of cases where two programs read the same text and disagreed.

sections.title: The Grammar and Its Six Structural Characters
sections.content:
A JSON text is a sequence of tokens. The set of tokens includes six structural characters, strings, numbers and three literal names, and a JSON text is a serialized value. Certain previous specifications of JSON constrained a JSON text to be an object or an array; implementations that generate only objects or arrays where a JSON text is called for will be interoperable, because all implementations accept these as conforming JSON texts.

The grammar is given as JSON-text = ws value ws. The six structural characters are the left square bracket that begins an array, the left curly bracket that begins an object, the right square bracket that ends an array, the right curly bracket that ends an object, the colon that separates a name from a value, and the comma that separates one value from the next. Insignificant whitespace is allowed before or after any of the six structural characters, and the whitespace production covers the space, the horizontal tab, the line feed and the carriage return.

The grammatical rules in the document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 5234.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole format is one value, optionally wrapped in whitespace. Six punctuation marks do the structural work: two kinds of bracket and two kinds of brace, a colon and a comma. Spaces, tabs and line breaks are ignored between them.

sections.title: Values, Objects and Arrays
sections.content:
A JSON value MUST be an object, array, number or string, or one of three literal names: false, null and true. The literal names MUST be lowercase and no other literal names are allowed.

An object is a pair of curly brackets surrounding zero or more name/value pairs, or members. A name is a string, a single colon comes after each name separating it from the value, and a single comma separates a value from a following name. The names within an object SHOULD be unique. An object whose names are all unique is interoperable, because all software implementations receiving that object will agree on the name-value mappings. When the names are not unique the behaviour of software receiving the object is unpredictable: many implementations report the last name/value pair only, other implementations report an error or fail to parse the object, and some report all of the name/value pairs including duplicates. JSON parsing libraries have also been observed to differ as to whether they make the ordering of object members visible to calling software, and implementations whose behaviour does not depend on member ordering will be interoperable because they will not be affected by these differences.

An array is a structure of square brackets surrounding zero or more values, or elements, separated by commas. There is no requirement that the values in an array be of the same type.
sections.plainLanguage: An object is a set of labelled values, and the labels should be unique because otherwise different programs pick different winners. An array is a plain list, and the items in it do not have to be the same kind. The order of the members of an object is not part of the format, so a program must not rely on it.

sections.title: Numbers and Strings
sections.content:
A number is represented in base 10 using decimal digits. It contains an integer component that may be prefixed with an optional minus sign, which may be followed by a fraction part and or an exponent part. Leading zeros are not allowed. A fraction part is a decimal point followed by one or more digits. An exponent part begins with the letter E in upper or lower case, which may be followed by a plus or minus sign, and the E and optional sign are followed by one or more digits. Numeric values that cannot be represented in the grammar, such as Infinity and NaN, are not permitted.

The specification allows implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted. Since software implementing IEEE 754-2008 binary64, or double precision, numbers is generally available and widely used, good interoperability can be achieved by implementations that expect no more precision or range than these provide. A JSON number such as 1E400 or 3.141592653589793238462643383279 may indicate potential interoperability problems, since it suggests that the software that created it expects receiving software to have greater capabilities for numeric magnitude and precision than is widely available. When such software is used, numbers that are integers and are in the range from -(2^53)+1 to (2^53)-1 are interoperable, because implementations will agree exactly on their numeric values.

A string begins and ends with quotation marks. All Unicode characters may be placed within the quotation marks, except the characters that must be escaped: the quotation mark, the reverse solidus, and the control characters U+0000 through U+001F. Any character may be escaped. A character in the Basic Multilingual Plane, U+0000 through U+FFFF, may be represented as a six-character sequence: a reverse solidus, the lowercase letter u, and four hexadecimal digits encoding the code point, with the hexadecimal letters A through F in either case. Alternatively, there are two-character escape representations of some popular characters. To escape an extended character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, the character is represented as a 12-character sequence encoding the UTF-16 surrogate pair.

JSON text SHALL be encoded in UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32, and the default encoding is UTF-8, because there are many implementations that cannot successfully read texts in other encodings. Implementations MUST NOT add a byte order mark to the beginning of a JSON text, though implementations that parse JSON texts MAY ignore its presence rather than treating it as an error. The RFC also notes that the grammar allows member names and string values to contain bit sequences that cannot encode Unicode characters, for example a single unpaired UTF-16 surrogate, that such instances have been observed when a library truncates a UTF-16 string without checking whether the truncation split a surrogate pair, and that the behaviour of software receiving such values is unpredictable.
sections.plainLanguage: Numbers are plain decimals, with no leading zeros and no Infinity or NaN. Values that are whole numbers and fit in 53 bits either way round are safe to pass between programs. Strings hold any Unicode text, and a few characters have to be written as escapes. The file itself is normally UTF-8 and must not start with a byte order mark.

sections.title: Parsers and Generators
sections.content:
A JSON parser transforms a JSON text into another representation. A JSON parser MUST accept all texts that conform to the JSON grammar, and MAY accept non-JSON forms or extensions. An implementation may set limits on the size of texts that it accepts, on the maximum depth of nesting, on the range and precision of numbers, and on the length and character contents of strings.

A JSON generator produces JSON text, and the resulting text MUST strictly conform to the JSON grammar.

The RFC also gives guidance on string comparison. Software implementations are typically required to test names of object members for equality. Implementations that transform the textual representation into sequences of Unicode code units and then perform the comparison numerically, code unit by code unit, are interoperable, because implementations will agree in all cases on equality or inequality of two strings. Implementations that compare strings with escaped characters unconverted may incorrectly find that two strings which are really the same are not equal.
sections.plainLanguage: A parser has to accept every valid JSON text, and may accept more. A generator has to produce only valid JSON text. Both are allowed to set limits on how big or deep a document they will handle. One trap the RFC calls out is comparing strings before turning escapes back into characters, which makes two equal strings look different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Generally, there are security issues with scripting languages. JSON is a subset of JavaScript but excludes assignment and invocation.

Since JSON's syntax is borrowed from JavaScript, it is possible to use that language's eval() function to parse JSON texts. This generally constitutes an unacceptable security risk, since the text could contain executable code along with data declarations. The same consideration applies to the use of eval()-like functions in any other programming language in which JSON texts conform to that language's syntax.

The media type registration notes that JSON has been used to exchange data between applications written in many programming languages, that no charset parameter is defined, and that adding one really has no effect on compliant recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: JSON contains no commands, only data. The danger is that a programmer hands a JSON text to a language's eval function, which will run anything in it. Parse it with a JSON parser instead.

viz.caption: THE SIX KINDS OF JSON VALUE

items.title: object
items.text: A set of name/value pairs in curly brackets. The names should be unique.

items.title: array
items.text: An ordered list of values in square brackets. The values need not be the same type.

items.title: string
items.text: A sequence of Unicode characters inside quotation marks.

items.title: number
items.text: A decimal number, optionally signed, with an optional fraction and exponent.

items.title: true and false
items.text: The two boolean literals, written in lower case.

items.title: null
items.text: The literal used for an absent value.

items.label: name-separator
items.desc: Separates a name from its value.

items.label: value-separator
items.desc: Separates one value from the next.

viz.caption: WHAT A PARSER AND A GENERATOR MUST DO

cells: MUST accept all texts that conform to the JSON grammar. MAY accept non-JSON forms or extensions.
The resulting text MUST strictly conform to the JSON grammar.
